title: Overseers, Deacons, and the Mystery of Godliness
summary: Paul lists the qualities required of an overseer, a leader of the church, stressing character, household management, maturity, and a good reputation, and then the qualities required of deacons and of the women mentioned with them. He explains that he is writing so that Timothy will know how people should conduct themselves in God's household, the church of the living God. The chapter closes with a short hymn about Christ, the mystery of godliness.
story: After instructions on prayer and conduct in worship (chapter 2), Paul turns to leadership. The false teachers in Ephesus seem to have included men who wanted to be teachers (1:7), and the remedy is to make sure the church's leaders are people of tested character who hold to the truth. This is the fullest description of church leaders in the New Testament, and it has a close parallel in Titus 1:5-9. The chapter then steps back to name what the whole letter is for (verses 14-15) and ends with praise of Christ. The church's order serves its message: God's household holds up the truth about the one who appeared in the flesh.
historical:
The first churches borrowed and adapted forms of leadership from their world. Jewish synagogues were led by elders, and Greek associations and cities had officers called overseers who supervised affairs. In the New Testament, the words elder (presbuteros) and overseer (episkopos) appear to describe the same leaders: Paul summoned the elders of Ephesus and told them the Holy Spirit had made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5-7 uses the two terms for the same group. Churches seem to have had a plurality of elders together with deacons (Philippians 1:1). By the early second century, the letters of Ignatius of Antioch show a single bishop presiding over the elders and deacons in many churches, but that arrangement is not clearly visible here.

This is one reason the dating of the Pastoral Letters matters to scholars. Those who think a later follower of Paul wrote them see the church order as more developed than in Paul's lifetime; those who hold to Paul's authorship answer that the structure is simple, with no single bishop, and consistent with what Acts and Philippians describe. Deacons (from diakonos, servant) appear here as a recognized group with their own qualifications. Around AD 112, the Roman governor Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan that he had interrogated two slave women whom the Christians called ministers, a sign that women served in some recognized capacity in at least some churches by then.
cultural:
Almost everything on Paul's list would have been recognized by pagan moral writers as the marks of a respectable person: self-control, temperance, hospitality, freedom from drunkenness and violence, good household management. Paul's point is not that Christian leaders should have exotic virtues but that they must actually possess the ordinary ones that everyone admires, so that outsiders cannot accuse the church (verse 7). Two items stand out as distinctively Christian: the overseer must be “able to teach” (verse 2), and must not be a recent convert (verse 6).

The household was the basic unit of ancient society and included the extended family, dependents, and slaves. Managing it well was a public test of character, and the church itself met in homes. So Paul reasons from the smaller to the larger: a man who cannot care for his own household cannot care for God's (verse 5). Hospitality, too, mattered greatly in a world of few inns, where traveling believers and missionaries depended on the homes of church members. The overseer's home would be open.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-7 give the qualifications of an overseer, introduced as the second of the letter's “trustworthy sayings.” The list is not a job description; it is a portrait of character, framed at beginning and end by concern for reputation (“above reproach” in verse 2, a good reputation with outsiders in verse 7). Verses 8-13 follow the same pattern for deacons, with the word “likewise” marking each new group (verses 8 and 11). Verses 14-16 are a turning point in the letter, stating its purpose and ending with what appears to be an early Christian hymn or creed. It has six short lines arranged in three pairs that contrast earth and heaven: flesh and Spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. The chapter moves from the people who lead the church to the Christ the church confesses.

outline.t: The overseer: a noble task and the character it requires
The women: dignified, temperate, and faithful
Why Paul writes: conduct in God's household
The mystery of godliness: a hymn to Christ

doctrines.note: The church is “God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (verse 15). It does not create the truth but holds it up and makes it visible, and it needs leaders whose lives match what it proclaims.

The hymn of verse 16 traces Christ from incarnation (“He appeared in the flesh”) through his vindication by the Spirit, most likely in the resurrection, to his proclamation among the nations and his ascension (“was taken up in glory”).
Leadership in the church rests on character before skill. Of all the qualifications, only one, the ability to teach, is a gift; the rest describe a tested and consistent life.

words.note: Episkopos, overseer, from a verb meaning to look over or watch over. Older English versions render it “bishop,” but in the New Testament it names a local church leader, apparently the same person called an elder. The word stresses the leader's task of watchful care for the flock (compare Acts 20:28).

Diakonos, servant or minister, the ordinary word for someone who waits on others or carries out an assignment. Jesus used the related verb of himself (Mark 10:45). Here it has become the name of a recognized group in the church, though the text says little about their specific duties.

Mustērion, mystery. In Paul it does not mean a puzzle but something once hidden in God's purpose and now revealed. Deacons must hold to “the mystery of the faith” (verse 9), and verse 16 names the content of that mystery: the story of Christ.

Stulos, pillar. Ephesus was famous for the many columns of the temple of Artemis. Paul calls the church a pillar of the truth, together with its foundation (verse 15): a structure that supports and displays the truth to the world.

christ: The chapter's lists of qualifications lead to a hymn about Christ, and the order is deliberate. The church's leaders, however carefully chosen, exist to serve the “mystery of godliness,” which turns out to be a person. He appeared in the flesh, which confesses his true humanity and implies his existence before his birth. He was vindicated by the Spirit, most likely a reference to the resurrection, where God declared him righteous after the world had condemned him. He was seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory. In six lines the hymn covers the incarnation, resurrection, ascension, and the church's mission. The qualifications for leaders also echo Christ's own character, the servant who was gentle, not violent, and not a lover of money.

hard.q: Must overseers be men, and were there women deacons?
hard.a:
Both are second-order questions on which faithful Christians differ.

On overseers, the requirement that an overseer be “the husband of but one wife” (verse 2) is read in several ways even apart from the question of gender: a man faithful in marriage (literally a one-woman man), a ban on polygamy, a ban on remarriage after divorce, or a requirement that the leader be married. The complementarian reading holds that the office of overseer is reserved for qualified men. It notes that the qualification is stated in male terms, that the chapter follows directly on 2:12, where Paul restricts women from teaching and exercising authority over men, and that the overseer's task centers on teaching and governing. The egalitarian reading holds that Paul describes the typical case of his time without excluding women permanently. It notes that verse 1 opens with a general “If anyone”, that the phrase about one wife targets unfaithfulness rather than gender, much as the same phrase for widows in 5:9 targets faithfulness, and that restrictions in 2:12 were tied to the Ephesian situation.

On deacons, verse 11 speaks of “the women” in the middle of the deacon section. One reading takes them as deacons' wives: they are introduced between two sections about male deacons, and verse 12 returns at once to deacons as husbands. The other takes them as women deacons: the word “likewise” introduces a new group in verse 8 and again in verse 11, the Greek lacks a word for “their,” Phoebe is called a deacon (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), and Pliny's letter shows women ministers in the early second century. Readers should weigh both main readings in their strongest form.

questions: Most of the qualities in this chapter are ordinary virtues, not spectacular gifts. Why might God care so much that church leaders are consistent in ordinary things?
What would it look like for your church to be the pillar and foundation of the truth in your community?
Read the hymn of verse 16 aloud. Which line of the story of Christ do you most need to remember this week, and why?
